notes.b: Views of development differ on what counts as progress and on who sets the standard.
points: Economic development means growth in a country's output and income, usually measured by GNP per head.
Human development means health, education, freedom and choice: people's ability to live lives they value.
Sustainable development means meeting today's needs without harming the future.
Who defines development matters: definitions are usually set by rich countries and international institutions, which decides which goals and measures count.
Measures follow views: GNP per head reflects the growth view and the HDI reflects the human view. The Economic Development notes cover both measures in full.
'Underdevelopment' has two meanings. It can mean 'not yet developed', the modernisation view, or 'made poor by others', the dependency view. Both meanings must be explained.

notes.h: How views have changed over time
notes.b: Each era produced its own model of development and its own goals.
points: Colonial era: colonies were treated as suppliers of raw materials, and colonial rule was justified by a 'civilising mission'.
1950s–60s: growth and modernisation. Development meant GNP growth and industrialisation, following Rostow's model.
1960s–70s: dependency theory emerged in Latin America, arguing that poverty was caused by the structure of the world economy.
1970s: the basic needs approach put food, water, shelter, health and education ahead of GNP growth.

1980s–90s: the neoliberal Washington Consensus. The term was coined by the economist John Williamson in 1989 for market reforms (privatisation, free trade and cuts in state spending) promoted by the IMF, World Bank and US Treasury.
From 1990: human development, measured by the HDI, and the idea of development as freedom.
From 1987: sustainable development, which links growth to environmental limits.
2000s–2010s: goal-based views (the Millennium and Sustainable Development Goals) and rights-based views of development.

notes.b: Environmental determinism holds that the physical environment, especially climate, decides how far a society can develop.
points: Temperate climates were said to produce energetic, advanced peoples, while tropical climates were said to produce poor and backward societies.

The theory was developed by 19th- and early 20th-century geographers. Ellen Churchill Semple, in Influences of Geographic Environment (1911), and Ellsworth Huntington, in Civilization and Climate (1915), argued that climate determined how 'civilised' a people could become.
It was used to justify colonialism and racial hierarchies, presenting European rule as the natural order.
Critique: it ignores history, including colonialism, slavery and trade rules, as well as politics and people's choices.
Critique: it is contradicted by Singapore, which is tropical yet one of the world's richest countries, and by poverty in temperate places.
Critique: its assumptions about the abilities of different peoples were racist, and they are rejected today.
Reply: possibilism, associated with the French geographer Paul Vidal de la Blache, holds that the environment offers possibilities and people choose which to use.

notes.h: A softer modern version: geography matters
points: Jeffrey Sachs, in The End of Poverty (2005), stressed malaria, poor soils and a landlocked location as obstacles that aid could help overcome.
Jared Diamond, in Guns, Germs, and Steel (1997), argued that geography (crops, animals and the east–west axis of Eurasia) explains why some societies gained power first.

Botswana is landlocked, yet it became independent in 1966 as one of the world's poorest countries. Diamonds and stable government made it an upper-middle-income country, so physical limits can be overcome.
Physical factors raise the costs of development without fixing its outcome.

notes.b: Modernisation theory holds that all societies pass along one path from traditional to modern, as Western Europe and North America did. Poor countries are behind and need investment, technology, industry and Western values to catch up.
points: Walt W. Rostow, an American economist and adviser to Presidents Kennedy and Johnson, set out his five-stage model in The Stages of Economic Growth: A Non-Communist Manifesto (1960).
Stage 1, traditional society: subsistence farming and limited technology.
Stage 2, preconditions for take-off: investment in transport and education, new ideas, and trade opening to outside contact.
Stage 3, take-off: investment rises to over 10% of national income and a few leading industries grow fast.
Stage 4, drive to maturity: growth spreads across the economy and diversifies into many industries.
Stage 5, age of high mass consumption: most people enjoy cars, durable goods and services.
Rostow dated Britain's take-off to the late 18th century (about 1783–1802). He is not used to date any other country's take-off.

notes.b: Applying Rostow to Ireland is a textbook interpretation, not Rostow's own work. The model can be applied to Irish development as follows.
points: Traditional stage: a farming economy with heavy emigration, including net emigration of about 400,000 between 1951 and 1961.
Preconditions: T. K. Whitaker's Economic Development and the First Programme for Economic Expansion (1958), and an opening to foreign investment, with the IDA set up in 1949.
Take-off: industrial growth in the 1960s and 1970s, free secondary education from 1967, and EEC membership from 1 January 1973.
Drive to maturity: growth in the 1980s and 1990s led by multinational companies.
High mass consumption: the Celtic Tiger, from the mid-1990s to 2007.
Limits of the model: the crash from 2008 and the EU–IMF bailout of November 2010 show that the stages can be reversed.
The Korean War (1950–53) left South Korea among the world's poorest countries.
Export-led industrialisation was planned under Park Chung-hee from the 1960s.
Large family conglomerates (chaebol), such as Samsung, Hyundai and LG, led the growth, and heavy investment in education supplied skilled workers.
South Korea joined the OECD in 1996 and was reclassified as a developed country by UNCTAD in 2021.
Its rapid industrialisation seems to fit Rostow's stages, which is why it is used as evidence for the model.
Eurocentric: it assumes the Western path is the only path and that Western society is the goal.

Linear and stage-bound: countries can skip, stall or go backwards. Zimbabwe, with land seizures from 2000 and hyperinflation peaking in 2008, and Syria, where civil war from 2011 reversed decades of progress, show this.
It ignores colonialism and unequal trade as causes of poverty.
It assumes wealth will trickle down from growth to the poor, which often does not happen.
It is growth-centred and environmentally unsustainable: mass consumption for everyone is impossible on current resources.
It ignores culture, inequality and gender.
Many African states that followed modernisation advice did not take off.
Large prestige projects, such as dams and steelworks, were built to bring industry quickly, often with little local participation.
The Washington Consensus described above applied the same top-down thinking through markets, imposing reforms from outside.
Debt and aid, which followed these policies, are covered in the Empowering People notes.

notes.b: Dependency theory holds that poor countries are poor because of how they were drawn into the world economy, not because of their own backwardness.
points: The rich core (metropolis) countries develop by draining wealth from the poor periphery (satellite) countries.
Development of the core and underdevelopment of the periphery are two sides of one process.
Origins: Latin American economists and thinkers. Raúl Prebisch, an Argentine economist, headed the UN Economic Commission for Latin America (ECLA), set up in 1948.
With Hans Singer, Prebisch argued in 1950 that the terms of trade of primary-product exporters tend to decline (the Prebisch–Singer thesis).
Andre Gunder Frank, in The Development of Underdevelopment (1966), argued that Latin America was underdeveloped by its links with the core, through metropolis–satellite chains.
Dependency is structural, through trade, investment and debt. It is not the same as dependence on aid.
Colonial extraction of raw materials, using slavery where needed.
Dependence on one or two primary exports whose prices are low and unstable.
Tariff escalation, where rich countries tax processed goods more heavily than raw materials, and rich-country subsidies that undercut producers.
Profit repatriation: multinationals send profits home.
Debt repayments drain income that could fund development.
Brain drain: skilled people leave for the core.
Local elites who benefit from the link with the core and resist change.

notes.h: Dependency applied: Latin America and African commodity exporters
points: Brazil's colonial economy moved through export cycles of brazilwood, sugar, gold, coffee and rubber, each tied to demand in the core.
Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana grow over half of the world's cocoa, mostly exported as beans rather than processed chocolate.
Zambia depends on copper, which is most of its exports.
Sudan's Gezira Scheme, from 1925, grew cotton for the Lancashire mills.
Immanuel Wallerstein's The Modern World-System (first volume 1974) divides the world into core, semi-periphery and periphery.
Core countries control high-value production and finance. Periphery countries supply cheap raw materials and labour.
Semi-periphery countries sit between the two, and countries can move between zones. South Korea and China have moved up.
China began reforms in 1978, joined the WTO in 2001 and has been the world's second-largest economy since 2010.
It cannot explain how the Asian Tigers (South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Singapore) and China developed through trade with the core.
Countries that cut their links with the world economy through self-reliance stayed poor.
It blames outside forces and can excuse corruption and poor government at home.
The remedy, withdrawal from world trade, has rarely worked.
The basic needs approach of the 1970s put food, water, shelter, health and education first, not GNP growth.
The ILO World Employment Conference (1976) put basic needs at the centre of development policy.
E. F. Schumacher's Small Is Beautiful (1973) argued for small-scale, appropriate technology that local people can afford, use and repair.
Schumacher founded the Intermediate Technology Development Group in 1966, now called Practical Action.
Amartya Sen, an Indian economist and Nobel Prize winner in Economics (1998), argued in Development as Freedom (1999) that development means widening people's choices and capabilities.
The first Human Development Report (UNDP) appeared in 1990. The HDI was created by Mahbub ul Haq with Sen; see the Economic Development notes for how it works.
The human view judges progress by people's lives, not by national output alone.
Bottom-up (grassroots) development puts participation, co-operatives, NGOs and women's groups at the centre, in contrast to top-down projects. See the Empowering People notes.
The Brundtland Report, Our Common Future (1987), set out sustainable development. See the Sustainable Development notes for its application.
The Sustainable Development Goals are 17 goals adopted in 2015, with a target year of 2030.
Bhutan's Gross National Happiness was put forward in the 1970s by King Jigme Singye Wangchuck as a goal ahead of GNP.

Hans Rosling, with Ola Rosling and Anna Rosling Rönnlund in Factfulness (2018), argued that dividing the world into 'developed' and 'developing' is out of date and replaced it with four income levels.
Famine, war, disease and helpless victims, especially children, dominate media and charity images of Africa. Good news and ordinary life are rarely shown.
Stereotypes follow, such as the belief that 'Africa is a country'.
Donors can take a 'saviour' view of themselves, and the people shown can come to see themselves as helpless.
Investors and tourists may lose confidence in countries shown only as crisis zones.
Audiences can tire of the same images, leading to donor fatigue.
A BBC television report by Michael Buerk in October 1984 brought the famine to world attention.
Band Aid's single 'Do They Know It's Christmas?' (1984) and the Live Aid concerts (July 1985), organised by Bob Geldof, raised huge sums.
The famine came during civil war in northern Ethiopia, and government policies worsened it.
The powerful coverage fixed an image of Africa as helpless and dependent, and hid the political causes: civil war and government policy.
Dóchas, the Irish association of development NGOs, drew up a Code of Conduct on Images and Messages that its member organisations sign.
The code requires images to respect the dignity of the people shown, avoid stereotypes and tell the full context.
NGOs use dignified images and the people's own voices in their appeals.
Kenyan writer Binyavanga Wainaina's satirical essay 'How to Write About Africa' (Granta, 2005) mocked Western clichés about the continent.
Nigerian novelist Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie's talk 'The Danger of a Single Story' (2009) argued that a single story about a place distorts it.

Rwanda: after the genocide from 7 April 1994, in which about 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi, were killed in about 100 days, the country rebuilt. Since the 2013 election women have held over 60% of the seats in the lower house of parliament, the highest share of any country.

Kenya: M-Pesa, a mobile-phone money transfer service launched in 2007 by Safaricom (part-owned by Vodafone), lets people without bank accounts send, receive and save money by text message. Most Kenyan adults use it.
Botswana: its growth from diamonds under stable government is the counter-image to the landlocked-state argument above.
'Underdeveloped' and 'backward' imply that poor societies are lagging behind a normal path.
'Primitive' implies that poor societies are at an earlier stage of human history.
'Developing' implies one direction of travel, towards the Western model.
'Less economically developed country' (LEDC) still measures other countries against the developed norm.
'Global South' groups countries by their position in the world economy rather than by wealth.
'Majority world' is a term popularised by the Bangladeshi photographer Shahidul Alam, because most of the world's people live there.
The UN created the 'least developed countries' category in 1971. Most of its members are in sub-Saharan Africa, and it is an official term.

notes.h: First World, Second World and Third World
points: 'Third World' was coined by the French demographer Alfred Sauvy in 1952, by comparison with the 'Third Estate' of the French Revolution.
It was originally a Cold War political term, not a ranking of wealth. The First World was the USA-led capitalist West and the Second World the Soviet-led communist bloc.
The Third World was the rest: mostly newly independent former colonies that did not align with either bloc.
The Bandung Conference, Indonesia, in April 1955 brought together leaders of newly independent Asian and African states. The Non-Aligned Movement was founded at Belgrade in 1961.
The Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991, ending the Second World and leaving the terms without their original meaning.
The terms became a ranking, with first meaning best, and a byword for poverty. They lump together very different countries, from Singapore to the poorest states.

notes.b: The North–South model divides the rich, industrialised North from the poor South.
points: The Brandt Report, North–South: A Programme for Survival (1980), came from a commission chaired by the former West German Chancellor Willy Brandt.
The Brandt Line runs roughly along 30°N and dips south to include Australia and New Zealand in the North.
The Brandt Line is a 1980 concept, not a current UN or World Bank classification.
The gap in income, health and power between most of Africa and Europe remains very large.
World Inequality Report 2022: the richest 10% of people own about 76% of global wealth, and the poorest half about 2%. Poverty and deprivation also exist within the North.
Global institutions remain weighted towards wealthy states: the five permanent members of the UN Security Council are the USA, the UK, France, Russia and China.

notes.h: Why the North–South model is outdated
points: Many 'South' countries are now high-income or industrial powers: Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan and Hong Kong.
China is the world's second-largest economy, and India is among the five largest.

The BRIC term was coined in 2001 by Jim O'Neill of Goldman Sachs, and the first BRIC summit was held in 2009. South Africa joined in 2011, forming BRICS. Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates joined in January 2024, and Indonesia in January 2025.
The G20, set up in 1999, includes China, India, Brazil, South Africa, Indonesia, Mexico and Saudi Arabia, giving the South a stronger voice.
Most of the world's people now live in middle-income countries, as Hans Rosling showed in Factfulness.
In 2016 the World Bank announced that it would stop dividing countries into 'developing' and 'developed' in its main data tables, keeping its four income groups.

notes.b: Eurocentric thinking sees the world from a European point of view and judges other societies by European standards, as if Europe's path, values and history were the norm.
points: The Mercator projection was designed by the Flemish map-maker Gerardus Mercator in 1569 for navigation, because lines of constant compass bearing are straight on it. Its effect is to place Europe at the top centre of the world map.
On the Mercator projection, Africa is about 14 times the area of Greenland, yet the two look similar in size.
The Peters (equal-area) projection, presented by the German historian Arno Peters in 1973 (the Gall–Peters projection), shows true areas and challenges this distortion.
Greenwich (London) was chosen as the prime meridian at the International Meridian Conference, Washington, in 1884.
Regional names such as 'Middle East' and 'Far East' are measured from Europe.
Christopher Columbus reached the Caribbean in 1492. Describing the Americas as discovered treats lands that were already inhabited as if they were empty.
At the Berlin Conference of 1884–85 European powers set the rules for claiming Africa, which they then divided among themselves. By 1914 only Ethiopia and Liberia were independent.
African and Asian achievements are ignored in European histories.
Edward Said's Orientalism (1978) showed how Western writing portrayed the East as exotic, backward and inferior.
'Developed' was defined as becoming like Western Europe, with industry, urbanisation and mass consumption.
Traditional knowledge and ways of life were dismissed, and Western experts designed projects without local input.
China's Belt and Road Initiative, launched in 2013, and the growth of South–South trade and aid, including China in Africa, show a shift away from European-led models.
The rise of Asia and the voices of local people now challenge Eurocentric models of development.

keyTerms.definition: Growth in a country's output and income, usually measured by GNP per head.
Improvement in health, education, freedom and choice, so that people can live lives they value.
Meeting today's needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs.
The view that the physical environment, especially climate, decides how far a society can develop; now discredited.
The view that the environment offers possibilities and that people choose which to use.
The view that all societies pass along one path from traditional to modern, as Western countries did.
Rostow's third stage, when investment rises above 10% of national income and a few leading industries grow fast.
The view that underdevelopment is caused by poor countries being drawn into an unequal world economy that drains their wealth to the core.
Core countries control high-value production and finance; periphery countries supply cheap raw materials and labour.
The ratio of the prices a country receives for its exports to the prices it pays for its imports.
A 1970s view that development should first meet food, water, shelter, health and education needs.
Small-scale technology that local people can afford, use and repair.
A 1980s–90s set of market reforms (privatisation, free trade, cuts in state spending) promoted by the IMF, World Bank and US Treasury.
Bhutan's measure of well-being, put forward in the 1970s as a goal ahead of GNP.
A Cold War term from 1952 for the mostly newly independent countries that were not part of the capitalist First World or the communist Second World.
A 1980 dividing line, running roughly along 30°N, that separates the rich North from the poor South.
Seeing the world from a European point of view and judging other societies by European standards.
A term for the countries where most of the world's people live, popularised by Shahidul Alam as an alternative to the 'developing world'.

factCards.term: How views of development have changed: the eras in order
factCards.definition: Colonial civilising mission; 1950s–60s modernisation (Rostow); 1960s–70s dependency theory; 1970s basic needs; 1980s–90s Washington Consensus (Williamson, 1989); sustainable development from 1987; human development from 1990; then goal- and rights-based views.

factCards.term: Underdevelopment: its two opposite meanings
factCards.definition: In the modernisation view it means 'not yet developed', a country behind on the same path. In the dependency view it means 'made poor by others', the result of being drained by the rich core.

factCards.term: Environmental determinism: what it claimed, who argued it, how it was used
factCards.definition: It claimed that climate decides how far a society can develop: temperate climates were said to make 'advanced' peoples, tropical ones poor. Ellen Churchill Semple (1911) and Ellsworth Huntington, Civilization and Climate (1915). It justified colonialism and racial hierarchies; now discredited.

factCards.term: Environmental determinism: four criticisms and the possibilist reply
factCards.definition: It ignores colonialism, slavery, trade rules and choice; tropical Singapore is rich, and landlocked Botswana reached upper-middle income through diamonds and stable government; temperate places can be poor; it is racist. Possibilism (Paul Vidal de la Blache): the environment offers choices.

factCards.term: Rostow's five stages of growth in order
factCards.definition: Traditional society (subsistence farming); preconditions for take-off (transport, education, trade); take-off (investment over 10% of national income, a few leading industries); drive to maturity; high mass consumption. Rostow, 1960.

factCards.term: Rostow's model applied to Ireland: a textbook reading

factCards.term: Rostow's model applied to South Korea
factCards.definition: The Korean War (1950–53) left it among the poorest countries; Park Chung-hee planned export-led industry from the 1960s; chaebol such as Samsung, Hyundai and LG and heavy education spending drove growth; OECD 1996; UNCTAD reclassified it as developed in 2021.

factCards.term: Modernisation theory: five criticisms
factCards.definition: Eurocentric, treating the Western path as the only one; linear, yet countries slip back (Zimbabwe's hyperinflation peaked in 2008; Syria's war from 2011); ignores colonialism and unequal trade; wealth often does not trickle down; mass consumption is unsustainable.

factCards.term: Dependency theory: who developed it and their key arguments
factCards.definition: Raúl Prebisch, head of ECLA (set up 1948), argued with Hans Singer (1950) that primary exporters' terms of trade decline. Andre Gunder Frank (1966): Latin America was underdeveloped by metropolis–satellite links to the core.

factCards.term: Dependency theory: seven ways the core drains the periphery
factCards.definition: Colonial extraction and slavery; dependence on one or two low-priced, unstable primary exports; tariff escalation and rich-country subsidies; multinationals sending profits home; debt repayments; brain drain; local elites who gain from the link.

factCards.term: Dependency theory: four examples of dependent economies
factCards.definition: Brazil's colonial export cycles (brazilwood, sugar, gold, coffee, rubber); Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana grow over half the world's cocoa, mostly sold as beans; Zambia relies on copper; Sudan's Gezira Scheme (from 1925) grew cotton for Lancashire.

factCards.term: Wallerstein's world-systems theory: three zones and movement
factCards.definition: Wallerstein, The Modern World-System (1974): the core controls high-value production and finance; the periphery supplies cheap materials and labour; the semi-periphery lies between. Countries move up: South Korea; China (reforms 1978, WTO 2001).

factCards.term: Dependency theory: four criticisms
factCards.definition: It cannot explain how the Asian Tigers and China grew by trading with the core; some countries that cut links through self-reliance stayed poor; it blames outside forces and can excuse corruption and poor government; withdrawal from world trade has rarely worked.

factCards.term: Basic needs and appropriate technology: names and dates
factCards.definition: Basic needs (1970s): food, water, shelter, health and education before GNP, made central by the ILO World Employment Conference (1976). E. F. Schumacher (Small Is Beautiful, 1973) founded what is now Practical Action in 1966, for appropriate technology.

factCards.term: Human development and other measures of well-being
factCards.definition: Amartya Sen, Development as Freedom (1999): development widens choices and capabilities; first Human Development Report, 1990. Bhutan's Gross National Happiness (1970s). Hans Rosling's Factfulness (2018): four income levels, not developed/developing.

factCards.term: Negative media images of Africa: five effects
factCards.definition: Famine, war and helpless victims dominate. Effects: stereotypes such as 'Africa is a country'; donors see themselves as saviours; the people shown may see themselves as helpless; investors and tourists lose confidence; audiences tire, causing donor fatigue.

factCards.term: Ethiopian famine 1984–85: how coverage shaped views of Africa
factCards.definition: Michael Buerk's BBC report (October 1984) led to Band Aid's single (1984) and Live Aid (July 1985), organised by Bob Geldof, raising huge sums. But it fixed an image of a helpless Africa and hid the causes: civil war in the north and government policy.

factCards.term: Three responses that challenge negative images of Africa
factCards.definition: The Dóchas Code of Conduct on Images and Messages, signed by Irish NGOs: respect dignity, avoid stereotypes, give context. Binyavanga Wainaina's satire How to Write About Africa (2005). Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie's talk The Danger of a Single Story (2009).

factCards.term: Three counter-images from sub-Saharan Africa
factCards.definition: Rwanda rebuilt after the 1994 genocide (about 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi, killed in about 100 days): since 2013 women have held over 60% of lower-house seats, the world's highest share. Kenya's M-Pesa (2007, Safaricom) lets people bank by text. Botswana: stable, diamond-funded growth.

factCards.term: Third World: who coined it, its Cold War meaning, why it is outdated
factCards.definition: Alfred Sauvy (1952), after the Third Estate: non-aligned former colonies outside the USA-led First and Soviet Second World (Bandung 1955; Non-Aligned Movement 1961). Outdated: the Soviet Union ended in 1991; it became a ranking; it lumps Singapore with Niger.

factCards.term: North–South divide: how the South has risen
factCards.definition: The Asian Tigers (South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore) are rich; China is second-largest, India top five. BRIC, coined in 2001 (summit 2009), added South Africa (2011), then Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates (2024) and Indonesia (2025).

factCards.term: North–South divide: three more reasons it is outdated
factCards.definition: The G20 (1999) includes China, India, Brazil, South Africa, Indonesia, Mexico and Saudi Arabia; most people now live in middle-income countries (Rosling); in 2016 the World Bank stopped dividing countries into developing and developed in its main data tables.

factCards.term: North–South divide: why the idea is still partly valid
factCards.definition: The income, health and power gap between most of Africa and Europe remains huge. Global wealth is very unequal: the richest 10% of people own about 76%, the poorest half about 2% (World Inequality Report 2022). Four of the five permanent Security Council seats are Northern: USA, UK, France, Russia.

factCards.term: Eurocentric maps: three examples and one challenge
factCards.definition: Mercator's 1569 projection, made for navigation, puts Europe top centre; Africa is about 14 times Greenland's area yet looks similar. Greenwich became the prime meridian (1884); 'Middle East' and 'Far East' are named from Europe. Challenge: Peters' equal-area projection (1973).

factCards.term: Eurocentric thinking in history and development: examples
factCards.definition: Columbus's 1492 'discovery' of inhabited lands; European powers set the rules for claiming Africa at the Berlin Conference (1884–85); Said's Orientalism (1978) on the East shown as backward; 'developed' meant becoming like Western Europe. China's Belt and Road (2013) marks a shift.

questions.prompt: Views of development and underdevelopment involve contrasting models and approaches to development. Discuss.
questions.model: (a) Rostow's modernisation model sees development as a five-stage path, from traditional society through preconditions, take-off, drive to maturity and high mass consumption. Rostow dated Britain's take-off to about 1783–1802. It can be applied to Ireland, with net emigration of about 400,000 between 1951 and 1961, the First Programme for Economic Expansion of 1958, free secondary education from 1967, EEC membership from 1 January 1973 and the Celtic Tiger from the mid-1990s; the textbook reading is only an interpretation. It can also be applied to South Korea, whose export-led industrialisation under Park Chung-hee from the 1960s and chaebol such as Samsung, Hyundai and LG fit the stages. Critique: it is Eurocentric and linear; Zimbabwe's land seizures from 2000 and Syria's civil war from 2011 show that countries can go backwards; it ignores colonialism and unequal trade; its trickle-down assumption often fails; and it is growth-centred and environmentally unsustainable. (b) Dependency theory argues that the core drains wealth from the periphery through trade, investment and debt. Raúl Prebisch and Hans Singer argued in 1950 that the terms of trade of primary exporters decline, and Andre Gunder Frank argued in 1966 that Latin America was underdeveloped by its links with the core. Examples: Brazil's colonial export cycles of brazilwood, sugar, gold, coffee and rubber; cocoa from Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana exported mostly as beans; Zambia's dependence on copper; and Sudan's Gezira cotton for Lancashire mills from 1925. Wallerstein's world-systems theory adds a semi-periphery and shows that countries can move between zones. Critique: it cannot explain the Asian Tigers or China's development through trade; countries that cut their links stayed poor; and it can excuse corruption at home. (c) Environmental determinism, associated with Ellen Churchill Semple (1911) and Ellsworth Huntington (1915), held that climate decided how civilised a people could become. It was used to justify colonialism and racial hierarchies. Critique: it ignores history and politics, Singapore is tropical yet one of the richest countries, and its assumptions were racist. Possibilism, associated with Paul Vidal de la Blache, replies that people choose among possibilities. (d) Bottom-up and human development views offer an alternative. The basic needs approach of the 1970s put food, water, shelter, health and education first. Schumacher's Small Is Beautiful (1973) argued for appropriate technology that local people can afford and repair. Amartya Sen's Development as Freedom (1999) defines development as widening people's choices and capabilities, and the HDI followed from the first Human Development Report in 1990. Evaluation: the contrasting models each explain part of the picture, but the human and bottom-up views best fit the evidence that growth alone does not reduce poverty or improve lives.

questions.prompt: Views of development and underdevelopment are subject to change and should be challenged. Discuss with reference to the idea of the developed 'North' and the developing 'South'.
questions.model: The Brandt Report of 1980 divided the world into a rich, industrialised North and a poor South, and the Brandt Line runs roughly along 30°N, dipping south to put Australia and New Zealand in the North. The division grew from Cold War ideas: Alfred Sauvy coined 'Third World' in 1952 as a political term for the mostly newly independent countries outside the USA-led First World and the Soviet-led Second World, and the Non-Aligned Movement was founded at Belgrade in 1961 after the Bandung Conference of 1955. The division is outdated. The Second World disappeared when the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991, and the terms became a ranking that lumps together very different countries. Many 'South' countries are now high-income or industrial powers, including Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan and Hong Kong. China is the world's second-largest economy and India is among the five largest. The BRICS group, which South Africa joined in 2011 and Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, the United Arab Emirates and Indonesia joined later, and the G20 give the South a stronger voice. Poverty and deprivation exist within the North, and most of the world's people live in middle-income countries, as Hans Rosling showed. The World Bank stopped dividing countries into developing and developed in its main data tables in 2016. What remains valid: the income, health and power gap between most of Africa and Europe is very large, and global institutions such as the UN Security Council, whose five permanent members are the USA, the UK, France, Russia and China, remain weighted towards wealthy states. Eurocentric thinking explains why the labels persist. The Mercator projection of 1569 places Europe at the top centre, and on it Greenland looks similar in size to Africa, which is about 14 times its area. The Peters projection of 1973 shows true areas. Development was defined as becoming like Western Europe, and European histories describe the Americas as discovered in 1492 and ignore African and Asian achievements. Edward Said's Orientalism (1978) showed how the East was portrayed as exotic, backward and inferior. Changing views are shown by China's Belt and Road Initiative from 2013 and South–South trade and aid. Evaluation: the North–South model is a useful reminder of inequality but a poor description of today's world, so the views must be challenged and updated.

questions.prompt: Explain how images and language used about developing countries can shape our view of development.
questions.model: Images of developing countries, especially sub-Saharan Africa, tend to show famine, war, disease and helpless victims, especially children, while good news and ordinary life are rarely shown. The 1984–85 Ethiopian famine shows the effect: the BBC report by Michael Buerk in October 1984 and Band Aid and Live Aid raised huge sums, but the coverage fixed an image of Africa as helpless and dependent and hid the political causes, civil war and government policy. Such images produce stereotypes such as 'Africa is a country', a saviour view of donors, lower confidence among investors and tourists, and donor fatigue. Loaded language reinforces this: 'underdeveloped', 'backward' and 'primitive' imply a lagging path, and 'developing' implies one direction of travel towards the Western model. Responses include the Dóchas Code of Conduct on Images and Messages, which requires images to respect people's dignity and show the full context. A counter-image is Kenya's M-Pesa, a mobile-phone money transfer service launched in 2007, which most Kenyan adults use, showing a different development story.
